summary: The CDNI Request Routing Redirection interface lets an upstream CDN ask whether a downstream CDN could handle a user request, and lets the downstream one advertise its footprint and capabilities. This proposed standard defines the redirection part so user requests can be sent to the best interconnected CDN.

plainLanguage.summary: If one pizza shop cannot deliver to your street, it can pass your order to a partner shop that can. This defines how the shops ask each other and answer.

questions: what is cdni request routing redirection
how do cdns redirect users to each other
what is cdn path in cdni
subtitle: How one CDN asks a partner CDN where to send a user's request, over a simple HTTP and JSON interface.

tldr.problem: When interconnected CDNs share the work of serving users, the CDN that receives a request (the upstream CDN) needs a standard way to ask a partner (the downstream CDN) whether it will take the request and where to send the user.
tldr.mechanism: The upstream CDN sends an HTTP POST carrying a JSON description of the user's DNS or HTTP request. The downstream CDN replies with a JSON body naming the redirection target, plus cacheability and scope information.
tldr.outcome: One interface covers both DNS and HTTP redirection, with error codes, caching rules and loop detection built in. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 7975 is a Proposed Standard from October 2016, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Redirection Interface Does
sections.content:
A Content Delivery Network (CDN) delivers content at scale by prefetching or caching it on distributed caching servers called surrogates. RFC 6707 describes the problem of interconnecting CDNs, and RFC 7336 splits the CDNI Request Routing interface into two parts: an asynchronous advertisement of footprint and capabilities by a downstream CDN (dCDN), and a synchronous exchange in which an upstream CDN (uCDN) asks whether a dCDN will accept a user request.

RFC 7975 defines only the second part, the Request Routing Redirection interface (RI). A user agent asks a request router in the uCDN for something using DNS or HTTP. The uCDN queries the dCDN, and the dCDN answers with a Redirection Target (RT), the endpoint the user agent should be sent to. The RT may be a surrogate or another request router, and the dCDN controls which one it provides.

The RI matters only for Recursive Request Redirection. Iterative redirection involves no RI exchange, so it is out of scope. How the uCDN learns the dCDN's RI URI (static configuration, discovery through the CDNI Control interface, or other means) is not specified.
sections.plainLanguage: The first shop gets your order but a partner shop is closer to you. The first shop calls the partner to ask, and the partner says who should bring it.

sections.title: One HTTP Interface for DNS and HTTP Redirection
sections.content:
The RI is a simple HTTP interface. The uCDN sends an HTTP POST to the dCDN's RI URI, with the attributes of the user's request wrapped in the body. The dCDN replies with an HTTP 200 whose body holds the RT attributes of the protocol-specific response to return, together with parameters for cacheability and scope. The uCDN then sends the user agent a DNS or HTTP redirection pointing at the RT.

The RFC gives reasons for using one interface for both kinds of redirection. Operators deploy, monitor and troubleshoot a single interface, and nobody has to proxy DNS, HTTP or RTMP requests or squeeze extra CDNI data into end-user requests. New redirection methods can be added later by defining more protocol-specific keys.

Request and response bodies are JSON objects that MUST conform to I-JSON (RFC 7493). Senders MUST write all specified keys in lowercase, and receivers MUST ignore unknown or invalid keys. Requests use the media type application/cdni with the payload type redirection-request, and responses use redirection-response.
sections.plainLanguage: All the shops use the same order form, whether the customer phoned or walked in. That way everyone only has to learn one form.

sections.title: Request and Response Messages
sections.content:
The top-level keys are dns, http, scope, error, cdn-path and max-hops. A message MUST contain only one of dns or http. Requests MUST contain cdn-path.

DNS redirection. The request dns dictionary MUST carry resolver-ip, qtype (A or AAAA), qclass and qname. It may carry c-subnet, the user's address or prefix, and dns-only, which forces the dCDN to answer with surrogates rather than another request router. A successful response MUST include rcode and name and at least one of a, aaaa or cname. A cname MUST NOT appear together with a or aaaa. An optional ttl defaults to 0.

HTTP redirection. The request http dictionary MUST carry c-ip, cs-uri, cs-method and cs-version, and may add selected headers as cs-(headername). The response MUST include sc-status (usually 302), sc-version, sc-reason, cs-uri and sc-(location). The uCDN MAY drop or alter any sc-(headername) values before replying to the user agent, and it is advised to think carefully before passing cache headers on, since doing so could let later requests bypass the uCDN.

Cookies SHOULD NOT normally be sent in RI requests, and a uCDN SHOULD only include information that is absolutely necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: The form has boxes for who is asking and what they want. The answer has boxes for where to go instead, like a note saying 'ask the shop on Elm Street'.

sections.title: Caching, Errors and Loop Prevention
sections.content:
An RI response may be cached by the uCDN using standard HTTP Cache-Control, and may be reused only when the user agent's request would produce an identical RI request, except for c-ip when it falls inside the response's scope. An optional scope dictionary with an iprange list of CIDR subnets tells the uCDN which other users the response also fits. With overlapping cached responses, the uCDN SHOULD use the most recent one.

RI responses SHOULD include an error dictionary with an error-code and optional reason when something fails. The first digit sets the class: 1xx informational, 4xx uCDN error, 5xx dCDN error, with 2xx and 3xx reserved. The RFC does not say what a uCDN must do on a given code.

To catch loops, every CDN MUST add its CDN Provider ID to cdn-path on each RI request it originates or cascades. A Provider ID looks like AS64496:0: the letters AS, the AS number, a colon and a qualifier. A dCDN MUST reject a request whose cdn-path already contains its own ID, and SHOULD use error 502. Transit CDNs MUST NOT propagate a request when the number of IDs in cdn-path is equal to or greater than max-hops, and a dCDN seeing more IDs than max-hops MUST send an error, SHOULD use 503. Setting max-hops to 1 stops propagation beyond the first dCDN. Loops in the data plane are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Each shop signs its name on the order slip. If a shop sees its own name already there, it knows the order is going in circles and says so.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
RI requests contain parts of the user's original request, notably the IP address and requested URI, and responses reveal the dCDN's policy about which surrogates serve which content and locations. A uCDN could also probe the dCDN's edge topology with repeated requests for different content and addresses, and a broad scope can make that easier.

Implementations MUST support TLS transport as per RFC 2818 and RFC 7230. Where protection is needed, mutually authenticated TLS MUST be used, following RFC 7525.

On privacy, the dCDN that finally gets the user learns the user's address anyway. A uCDN that checks several candidate dCDNs, however, exposes user addresses and URIs to candidates that are not chosen. Masking bits of the user's address is possible but reduces the usefulness of the RI, for example when users and resolvers sit behind a carrier-grade NAT.
sections.plainLanguage: The order slip has your address on it, so the shops pass it in a locked envelope and only tell each other what they need to.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered two payload types for the application/cdni media type, redirection-request and redirection-response. IANA also created a new subregistry, "CDNI RI Error response code", for the values of the error-code key. Codes must be three-digit integers, and new entries need Specification Required, with a Designated Expert checking that they do not duplicate existing codes and fit the error classes.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list where the error numbers are written down so everyone means the same thing by them.

messages.label: DNS or HTTP request
messages.note: CDN A decides CDN B may serve it best.

messages.label: Redirection response
messages.note: Points the user agent at the RT.

items.label: Informational
items.desc: Generic code carrying a human-readable string; not an error.

items.label: uCDN error
items.desc: The dCDN cannot or will not process the request because of a perceived uCDN error.

items.label: dCDN error
items.desc: The dCDN knows it has erred or cannot satisfy the request.

items.label: Unable to retrieve metadata
items.desc: The dCDN cannot get the metadata for the requested content.

items.label: Loop detected
items.desc: A redirection loop was found in cdn-path.

items.label: Maximum hops exceeded
items.desc: The number of hops exceeds max-hops.

items.label: Out of capacity
items.desc: The dCDN lacks capacity to handle the request.

items.label: Delivery protocol not supported
items.desc: The delivery protocols in the CDNI Metadata are not supported.

items.label: Redirection protocol not supported
items.desc: The requested redirection protocol is not supported, or dns-only is set and a surrogate RT cannot be returned.
